newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura's new president says aims to restore trust.
newsitem.headline: Nomura's new president says aims to restore trust.

text.p: The new president of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, Masashi Suzuki, said on taking over the post on Friday that the top priority was to restore trust in the company.
Suzuki, who is also Nomura's chairman, made the comment at a news conference at which Hideo Sakamaki said he was resigning as president effective from Friday.
Sakamaki said he was resigning to take responsibility for a scandal involving suspected illegal deals at the brokerage.
Sakamaki said he was becoming an adviser to the company, also effective on Friday.
Nomura will take all possible measures to avoid getting involved in similar scandals in the future, Suzuki said.

Suzuki told reporters he would take all possible steps to avoid any recurrence of scandals at the company. "My first priority is to restore confidence. I would like to transform the company to one with a healthy situation and transfer the company (management) to the next generation."

He made the comments at a news conference after Nomura said on Thursday last week that two of its directors apparently made discretionary transactions and funnelled profits from Nomura funds into a corporate client's account. Both actions contravene Japan's Securities Law.
Japanese media have reported that the client concerned was run by the brother of a former "sokaiya" racketeer, but Nomura has said it could not confirm the reports.
Asked if his presidency would be temporary, Suzuki did not make a clear comment, repeatedly saying he would transfer the company's management in a healthy condition to the next generation.
He also said the outcome of an investigation by Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission SESC), would affect his decision on Nomura's management.
He added that he would await the result of the SESC investigation to see whether other top executives in Nomura might be responsible for the scandal.
Former president Sakamaki said the scandal had not been systemic. He also said: "I have not met the corporate client concerned in the case at all."

Asked if more Nomura directors might be involved in the scandal, he said: "I do not think there are such things going on, but I don't know because I don't have any reports on that. The chief executive officer has responsibility for all kinds of things concerning the company."

He added: "As the head of a company which is responsible for what happens in markets, I thought it was important to (resign) from corporate management" to minimise the negative impact at a time when the company is being investigated by the SESC and cooperating in that investigation.

Sakamaki said: "I feel sorry and regretful because I will not be here to work in the stream of Japan's 'Big bang' financial reform, which aims at achieving an enhancement in Tokyo's presence in world markets."
New president Suzuki said Nomura had decided to accept an offer by two advisers -- Setsuya and Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation) -- to resign from the board.
Setsuya Tabuchi will take an honorary position with no involvement in the company management and without managing director status.
Yoshihisa Tabuchi will remain as an adviser but will resign as managing director.

Setsuya Tabuchi quit as Nomura chairman in 1991 after a scandal in which Nomura and other brokers reimbursed favoured clients for investment losses. Nomura said at the time that its affiliates had done deals with "yakuza" gangsters.
Yoshihisa Tabuchi quit as president at that time, also to take responsibility for the scandal.
Both returned to the board in 1995 in order to help Nomura deepen business ties with foreign clients.
Sakamaki replaced Yoshihisa Tabuchi in 1991 and had said repeatedly that Nomura must be "reborn" as a company whose priority is its customers' prosperity.
